# Tracking branches and upstream: -u, @{u}, and status

After this page you can set an upstream with `git push -u`, read the upstream tip as `@{u}`, interpret `git status -sb` ahead/behind counts, and fix a branch that has no upstream.

## Thesis

A local branch becomes useful for collaboration when it **tracks** a remote-tracking branch. Tracking stores two config keys (`branch.<name>.remote` and `branch.<name>.merge`) so `git pull`, `git push`, and `git status` know the default partner without you typing it every time.

Verified with **git 2.47.3**.

## Mental model

```text
  local feat  ──tracks──►  origin/feat  (remote-tracking ref)
       │                         │
       │                         └─ updated by fetch
       └─ your commits
```

`@{u}` means "the upstream of HEAD". `@{upstream}` is the long form.

## Lab

<!-- file: upstream-lab.sh -->
```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
rm -rf /tmp/up-demo && mkdir /tmp/up-demo && cd /tmp/up-demo
git init -b main
git config user.name t
git config user.email t@t
git commit --allow-empty -m a
git init --bare bare.git
git remote add origin "$(pwd)/bare.git"
git push -u origin main
git checkout -b feat
git commit --allow-empty -m f1
git push -u origin feat
git status -sb
git rev-parse --abbrev-ref '@{u}'
git config --get-regexp 'branch\.(main|feat)\.'
```

Verified output:

```text
## feat...origin/feat
?? bare.git/
?? out.txt
origin/feat
branch.main.remote origin
branch.main.merge refs/heads/main
branch.feat.remote origin
branch.feat.merge refs/heads/feat
```

## Everyday commands

```bash
git push -u origin HEAD          # set upstream to matching remote name
git branch -vv                   # see tracking and ahead/behind
git status -sb                   # ## feat...origin/feat [ahead 1]
git log @{u}..HEAD               # commits you have not pushed
git log HEAD..@{u}               # commits you have not merged/rebased
```

Unset or change:

```bash
git branch --unset-upstream
git branch -u origin/other
```

`branch.autoSetupMerge` / `push.autoSetupRemote` (newer Git) can create tracking automatically on first push — know what your version defaults to.

## Pitfalls

1. Pushing without `-u` then wondering why `git status` does not show ahead/behind.
2. Tracking a remote branch that was deleted — `git fetch --prune` then fix upstream.
3. Confusing the remote-tracking name `origin/feat` with the remote URL.
4. Using `@{u}` when no upstream is set — Git errors; set one first.

## Summary

- `push -u` records remote + merge ref for the current branch.
- `@{u}` is shorthand for that upstream tip.
- Status and pull/push defaults depend on tracking — set it deliberately.


## Worked scenarios

### Scenario A — first push of a feature branch
```bash
git switch -c feat/login
# ... commits ...
git push -u origin HEAD
```

Thereafter `git push` / `git pull` need no remote arguments.

### Scenario B — see what you are about to push
```bash
git log --oneline @{u}..HEAD
git diff @{u}
```

### Scenario C — recover after someone deleted the remote branch
```bash
git fetch --prune
git branch -vv
git branch -u origin/feat/login-v2
```

## Config keys

```text
branch.feat.remote = origin
branch.feat.merge  = refs/heads/feat
```

`git rev-parse --abbrev-ref @{u}` prints `origin/feat` when tracking is healthy.

## Common mistakes (extended)

- Creating a local branch named `origin/feat` by accident.
- Assuming `git pull` rebases because of tracking — pull behavior is `pull.rebase` / `--rebase`.
- Tracking `origin/main` from a feature branch "for convenience" — status becomes meaningless.
